```{r beta-importance}
#| tbl-cap: "What the open model's answer is actually sensitive to. Share of the variation in Longhill's modelled recruitment across the full sweep, by input."
env$importance %>%
  filter(term != "Residuals") %>%
  mutate(Input = recode(term,
    "w_spec" = "Which attractiveness specification",
    "factor(entry_year)" = "Which entry year",
    "site_label" = "Longhill's site",
    "factor(beta)" = "Distance decay (β)",
    "factor(gamma)" = "Strength of the catchment term (γ)")) %>%
  arrange(desc(pct)) %>%
  transmute(Input, `Share of the variation` = sprintf("%.1f%%", pct)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lr")
```

**Distance decay is not the big unknown.** It accounts for
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", env$importance$pct[env$importance$term == "factor(beta)"])`
of the variation in the answer, against
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", env$importance$pct[env$importance$term == "w_spec"])`
for how attractive each school is taken to be. That is worth knowing
because it says what data would be worth having: school-level revealed
preference, more than travel behaviour.

```{r fig-beta-sweep}
#| fig-cap: "Longhill's modelled recruitment across the swept range of distance decay, at each attractiveness specification, 2026. The vertical line is the value the model uses. The spread between the coloured lines is the attractiveness question; the slope along each line is the distance-decay question."
#| fig-height: 4.8
env$envelope %>%
  filter(entry_year == 2026, gamma == 1.6) %>%
  mutate(site = ifelse(site == "now", "Ovingdean (today)", "Elm Grove")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(beta, natural_intake, colour = w_label, group = w_label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = BETA, colour = "grey45", linetype = "31") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ site) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = NULL) +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(x = "Distance decay (β)", y = "Children recruited",
       title = "The slope along each line is what β decides",
       subtitle = "Longhill's recruitment with its own admission number unbinding, catchment term at 1.6") +
  theme_bh() + theme(legend.position = "top")
```

## What it looks like from one neighbourhood

```{r fig-beta-shares}
#| fig-cap: "One neighbourhood's children, shared between schools by journey time alone, at three values of the exponent. Attractiveness, catchment and capacity are all switched off here, so the only thing acting is distance."
#| fig-height: 4.6
zex <- costs %>% filter(zone == ex_zones$zone[1])
tidyr::expand_grid(beta = c(1.5, BETA, 3.2), zex) %>%
  group_by(beta) %>%
  mutate(share = cij^-beta / sum(cij^-beta),
         School = short_sch(name)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(lab = sprintf("β = %.1f", beta),
         School = forcats::fct_reorder(School, cij)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(share, School, fill = lab)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_percent()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("grey72", "#1f3b57", "grey45"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Share of the neighbourhood's children", y = NULL,
       title = sprintf("Distance alone, from %s", sub("[|].*$", "", ex_zones$zone[1])),
       subtitle = "Schools ordered by journey time. A steeper decay concentrates children on the nearest schools.") +
  theme_bh() + theme(legend.position = "top")
```

That is the whole of what the exponent does: at
`r sprintf("%.1f", 1.5)` the nearest school takes
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * with(zex, (cij^-1.5 / sum(cij^-1.5))[which.min(cij)]))`
of this neighbourhood's children on distance alone; at
`r sprintf("%.1f", 3.2)`, `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * with(zex, (cij^-3.2 / sum(cij^-3.2))[which.min(cij)]))`.

## A second decay, on a different scale

The four schools outside the city do not use $\beta$ at all. They are
chosen on straight-line kilometres with a decay of their own, fitted to
the published 2024 destinations:

$$\text{pull of an out-of-city school} \;=\; W^{\text{ext}}_j \; d_{ij}^{-`r sprintf("%.1f", ext$decay)`}$$

`r sprintf("%.1f", ext$decay)` is far steeper than
`r sprintf("%.1f", BETA)`, and the two are not comparable: this one is on
kilometres rather than minutes, and it is doing a different job. It is
absorbing everything that stops a Brighton family choosing a school in
another authority — the admissions arrangements of a different council,
the absence of a school bus, the sheer unfamiliarity — and compressing it
into the one dimension the fit has. It reproduces the published pattern,
which is a low bar for four schools and one year of data, and it should
not be read as a behavioural estimate at all.

## Checks you can run

```{r beta-checks}
#| tbl-cap: "What the decay should produce, and what it gives at the value the model uses."
r_now <- run_sim(inp, year = 2026, rules = list(rule = "priorities"))
m_now <- outcomes(inp, r_now)
tibble::tribble(
  ~Check, ~Result,
  "The exponent the model runs at",
  sprintf("%.1f, unchanged in every scenario", BETA),
  "Mean modelled journey to the school a child attends",
  sprintf("%.1f minutes", m_now$mean_min),
  "Against the national average school journey",
  sprintf("%.0f minutes (National Travel Survey)", acc$benchmarks$nts_min),
  "Share of children modelled at a school in their own catchment",
  sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * r_now$in_catch_share),
  "Sensitivity of the answer to the exponent",
  sprintf("%.0f%% of the variation in the sweep", env$importance$pct[env$importance$term == "factor(beta)"])) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lr")
```

The mean modelled journey sits above the national average, which is what
a city with a coastal edge and one school in the far east should produce.
If it came out at or below the national figure, either the decay or the
journey times would be wrong.

## What to be careful about

- **One exponent for the whole city.** Families differ in how far they
  will travel, and the literature is consistent that the willingness
  varies with income and with whether a car is available. A single
  $\beta$ averages over that, and it is the assumption most likely to
  matter for the equity questions in the strategic view.
- **Everything else is fitted *given* this value.** The attractiveness
  balancing (§3) and the catchment terms (§6) are estimated with $\beta$
  held at `r sprintf("%.1f", BETA)`. A different decay would give
  different fitted values for both, which is why the sweep re-runs the
  whole model rather than swapping the exponent at the end.
- **Time, not distance, and not cost.** A journey that is quick but
  requires two buses and a fare is treated as a short journey.
- **The floor at short journeys.** A power decay rises steeply as time
  approaches zero, so the very shortest journeys carry a lot of weight.
  The routed minimum in the table is
  `r sprintf("%.0f", min(costs$cij))` minutes, which keeps it in bounds.

## Questions this raises

1. Should $\beta$ vary between groups of families — by deprivation, or by
   whether a catchment has one school or two — rather than being one
   number for the city?
2. Is the power form right, or would an exponential decay fit the pattern
   of Brighton's journeys better? Both are standard; they differ most at
   the long-journey end, which is where the eastern questions sit.
3. Should the out-of-city decay be re-fitted once more than one year of
   destination data is available, or replaced by a proper choice model
   for schools in another authority?

# $\gamma_h$: how much living in the catchment counts {#sec-gamma}

```{r gamma-setup}
#| include: false
gam <- cal$gamma
gam_lab <- setNames(unname(CATCH_LABELS[CATCH_FROM_MODEL[names(gam)]]), names(gam))
r_now <- run_sim(inp, year = 2026, rules = list(rule = "priorities"))
```

## What it is

$\gamma_h$ is the bonus a school gets for being **in the family's own
catchment**. It sits in the exponent, so it multiplies a school's pull:

$$\text{pull} \;\propto\; W_j\, c_{ij}^{-\beta} \times
\begin{cases} e^{\gamma_{h(i)}} & \text{if } j \text{ is a school of } i\text{'s catchment}\\ 1 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

The subscript matters: $\gamma$ is indexed by **$h(i)$, the catchment the
family lives in**, not by the school. Stringer / Varndean families are
modelled as following their map more closely than Brighton Aldridge's
families follow theirs, and that is a statement about families rather
than about schools.

::: {.callout-important}

## This is about what families name, not about who gets admitted

Admission priority is a separate stage of the model (§9):
when a school is oversubscribed the council's criteria decide who is
offered a place, and living in the catchment is one of them. $\gamma_h$
is doing something different and earlier. It says how much more likely a
family is to **want** a school because it is the one their map points
them to — through habit, siblings, the school bus, or simply reading the
catchment as a statement about where their child belongs.

The distinction is why the strategic view can find that catchment
priority allocates nothing at an undersubscribed school while the
catchment still matters a great deal there: nobody is turned away, but
the map still shapes what families ask for.
:::

## The fitted values

```{r gamma-table}
#| tbl-cap: "The catchment term fitted for each catchment, and what it does to a school's pull. A term of 0 would mean the map makes no difference to what families name."
tibble(catchment = names(gam), gamma = as.numeric(gam)) %>%
  mutate(Catchment = unname(gam_lab[catchment]),
         `Fitted $\\gamma_h$` = sprintf("%.1f", gamma),
         `Multiplies a catchment school's pull by` = sprintf("%.1f×", exp(gamma))) %>%
  arrange(desc(gamma)) %>%
  select(Catchment, `Fitted $\\gamma_h$`, `Multiplies a catchment school's pull by`) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lrr")
```

```{r fig-gamma-map}
#| fig-cap: "The fitted catchment term by catchment. Darker is a population that follows its map more closely, once distance and attractiveness are accounted for."
#| fig-height: 5
gsf <- catch_sf %>%
  left_join(tibble(catchment = unname(CATCH_FROM_MODEL[names(gam)]),
                   gamma = as.numeric(gam)), by = "catchment")
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = gsf, aes(fill = gamma), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_sf(data = sch_sf, shape = 21, fill = "white", colour = "black", size = 2.6) +
  geom_sf_text(data = gsf %>% st_point_on_surface() %>% suppressWarnings(),
               aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", gamma)), size = 5, fontface = "bold",
               colour = "white", nudge_y = 0.006) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "mako", direction = -1, name = "γ") +
  coord_sf(expand = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "How closely each catchment's families follow their map",
       subtitle = "Fitted to the council's catchment-level preference table") +
  theme_void(12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#1f3b57"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey35"))
```

Stringer / Varndean, at `r sprintf("%.1f", gam[["DS_Varndean"]])`, and
Longhill, at `r sprintf("%.1f", gam[["Longhill"]])`, are the two most
attached populations in the city; Brighton Aldridge's, at
`r sprintf("%.1f", gam[["BACA"]])`, the least. Those two facts do much of
the work in every relocation and redraw result in the strategic view,
because a move trades one against the other.

## How they are fitted

The council's evidence to the Schools Adjudicator includes a
catchment-level preference table: how many first, second and third
preferences each catchment's children gave each school, pooled over
`r length(mt$calibrated$rounds)` rounds. That is a flow matrix — coarse,
but a matrix — and it is enough to fit one term per catchment.

The loop is:

1. Take the current catchment terms and **balance $W_j$** so the model
   reproduces each school's share of the city's first preferences (§3).
2. For one catchment, try every $\gamma$ on a grid from
   `r sprintf("%.0f", 0)` to `r sprintf("%.0f", 4)` in steps of 0.1,
   re-balancing $W_j$ at each step, and keep the value that minimises the
   **Poisson deviance** between the modelled and observed shares in that
   table.
3. Repeat for each catchment, then sweep again until nothing moves.

The deviance is the right loss here because the cells are counts of
preferences: it weights a cell by how many families it contains, so a
catchment that gives 400 first preferences counts for more than one that
gives 40.

```{r fig-gamma-profile}
#| fig-cap: "The fit against each candidate value, catchment by catchment. The point is the value chosen: the bottom of each curve. A flat curve would mean the data cannot distinguish one value from another."
#| fig-height: 5
cal$profile %>%
  mutate(Catchment = unname(gam_lab[catchment])) %>%
  group_by(Catchment) %>%
  mutate(rel = deviance - min(deviance)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot(aes(gamma, rel)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#1f3b57", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = ~ .x %>% group_by(Catchment) %>% slice_min(rel, n = 1),
             colour = "#d95f02", size = 2.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ Catchment, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Catchment term (γ)", y = "Deviance above the best fit",
       title = "Each catchment's own curve, and where it bottoms out",
       subtitle = "Lower is a better fit to the council's preference table") +
  theme_bh(11)
```

## What the fitting buys

```{r gamma-fit}
#| tbl-cap: "How well each specification reproduces the council's preference table. M4 is one catchment term for the whole city, fitted against offers; M5 is one per catchment, fitted against preferences."
cal$fit %>%
  transmute(Model = ifelse(model == "M4", "One term for the whole city (M4)",
                           "One term per catchment (M5)"),
            `Poisson deviance` = fmt_n(deviance),
            `Cell error (percentage points)` = sprintf("%.1f", cell_rmse_pp)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lrr")
```

```{r fig-gamma-own}
#| fig-cap: "The share of each catchment's first preferences that go to its own school or schools: what the council's table records, and what each specification produces."
#| fig-height: 4.6
cal$own %>%
  mutate(Catchment = unname(gam_lab[home])) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(observed, M4, M5), names_to = "src", values_to = "share") %>%
  mutate(src = recode(src, observed = "Observed",
                      M4 = "One term for the city", M5 = "One term per catchment"),
         src = factor(src, c("Observed", "One term for the city", "One term per catchment")),
         Catchment = forcats::fct_reorder(Catchment, share, .fun = max)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(share, Catchment, colour = src, shape = src)) +
  geom_point(size = 3.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#1f3b57", "grey65", "#d95f02"), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(16, 15, 17), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_percent()) +
  labs(x = "Share of the catchment's first preferences going to its own school", y = NULL,
       title = "A single city-wide term cannot reproduce the pattern",
       subtitle = "Fitting one term per catchment does, and it is the same model otherwise") +
  theme_bh() + theme(legend.position = "top")
```

The gain is large and it is concentrated where it matters. A single
city-wide term puts Stringer / Varndean's own-school share at
`r fmt_pct(100 * cal$own$M4[cal$own$home == "DS_Varndean"], 0)` against an
observed `r fmt_pct(100 * cal$own$observed[cal$own$home == "DS_Varndean"], 0)`,
and Longhill's at
`r fmt_pct(100 * cal$own$M4[cal$own$home == "Longhill"], 0)` against
`r fmt_pct(100 * cal$own$observed[cal$own$home == "Longhill"], 0)`. Fitting
each catchment separately reproduces both.

## The two schools with no catchment at all {#sec-gamma-faith}

```{r gamma-faith}
#| include: false
catch_lab <- function(x) {
  out <- unname(CATCH_LABELS[CATCH_FROM_MODEL[x]])
  dplyr::coalesce(out, x)
}
faith_n <- inp$schools$name[inp$schools$city & inp$schools$faith]
d_g <- r_now$flows
faith_rows <- d_g %>% filter(name %in% faith_n)
faith_mix <- d_g %>%
  filter(name %in% c(faith_n, "Varndean School", "Longhill High School")) %>%
  group_by(name, catchment) %>% summarise(n = sum(flow), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(name) %>% mutate(share = n / sum(n)) %>% ungroup()
faith_min <- d_g %>% group_by(name) %>%
  summarise(min = weighted.mean(cij, flow), n = sum(flow), .groups = "drop")
city_min <- faith_min %>%
  filter(name %in% inp$schools$name[inp$schools$city & !inp$schools$faith], n > 1)
faith_kern <- sum(inp$params$overflow[grepl(paste(faith_n, collapse = "|"),
                                            names(inp$params$overflow))])
```

Cardinal Newman and King's are in **no catchment**, on any of the maps
the simulator carries. That is not a simplification: neither school has
one. Admission to Cardinal Newman turns on Catholic baptism and practice,
and King's is a Church of England free school with its own criteria and
no geographic area attached.

So $\gamma_h$ never applies to them. Every one of the
`r fmt_n(nrow(faith_rows))` neighbourhood-to-faith-school pairs in the
model has the indicator $\mathbb{1}[\,i \in \text{catchment}(j)\,]$ set to
zero, and their pull is $W_j\, c_{ij}^{-\beta}\, C_j^{\delta}$ and nothing
else. Four consequences follow, and they are worth being explicit about:
between them these two schools take
`r fmt_pct(100 * sum(faith_rows$flow) / sum(d_g$flow))` of the city's
Year 7 children.

**Their attractiveness carries the religion.** A family's faith is not in
this model — no published dataset gives it by neighbourhood. What the
fitting sees is that a great many families across the whole city name
these schools first anyway, and the only term free to explain it is
$W_j$. So Cardinal Newman ends up with the highest attractiveness in the
city (`r sprintf("%.2f", W5[["Cardinal Newman Catholic School"]])` against
a mean of 1) and King's the second
(`r sprintf("%.2f", W5[["King's School"]])`). Read those two numbers as
"wanted, city-wide, for reasons the model does not contain" rather than
as a judgement of the school.

**Distance is the only thing holding them in place.** With no catchment
bonus, $c_{ij}^{-\beta}$ is the sole spatial control on where their
children come from — which is why they draw from everywhere and why
their intakes travel furthest:

```{r fig-gamma-faith}
#| fig-cap: "Where each school's intake comes from, by the family's home catchment. The two faith schools have no catchment of their own, so nothing anchors them to one part of the city."
#| fig-height: 4.4
faith_mix %>%
  mutate(School = short_sch(name),
         School = factor(School, c("Cardinal Newman", "King's", "Varndean", "Longhill")),
         Catchment = catch_lab(catchment)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(share, forcats::fct_rev(School), fill = Catchment)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = "Home catchment") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "Two schools drawn from the whole city, two from one corner of it",
       subtitle = "Modelled intake by the family's home catchment, 2026 entry") +
  theme_bh() + theme(legend.position = "right")
```

The children the model sends to King's travel
`r sprintf("%.0f", faith_min$min[faith_min$name == "King's School"])`
minutes on average and to Cardinal Newman
`r sprintf("%.0f", faith_min$min[faith_min$name == "Cardinal Newman Catholic School"])`,
against
`r sprintf("%.0f", min(city_min$min))` to
`r sprintf("%.0f", max(city_min$min))`
minutes at the eight community and academy schools. That is a real
feature of faith admissions, and the model reproduces it without being
told to.

**They are outside the catchment machinery everywhere else too.** The
priority-6 rule — a child from a single-school catchment applying outside
it — is defined on the catchment design, so it neither sends children to
these two nor gives them any standing there. When a boundary is redrawn
in a scenario, nothing about Cardinal Newman or King's changes except
through everyone else's movements. And because they are not community
schools, they are rationed by the proportional ceiling rather than by the
council's tiers (§9): the model has no representation of baptism
certificates or church attendance, so it treats an oversubscribed faith
school as a lottery over everyone who applied.

**They still take part in everything that is not the catchment.** They
compete in $C_j$ (§7) — Cardinal Newman is the second largest
contribution to Dorothy Stringer's competition term — they sit in every
neighbourhood's choice set and denominator (§8), and families do name
them as second preferences, so refused children are re-offered places
there: `r fmt_pct(100 * faith_kern / 6)` of a catchment's second
preferences go to one of the two on average (§10).

::: {.callout-warning}

## What this means for a faith-school scenario

Because the religion is inside $W_j$ rather than in a term of its own,
the simulator cannot distinguish "Cardinal Newman becomes less
attractive" from "fewer families in the city are practising Catholics".
Both are the same slider. A scenario that changes either should be read
as changing the *total* pull of the school, and the model will
redistribute those children by distance and catchment like anyone
else's — which is almost certainly too smooth a picture of what a
change in faith admissions would actually do.
:::

## What the slider does

The simulator's catchment slider multiplies **every** fitted term by the
same factor, from 0 to 2. At 0 the map stops mattering to what families
name and the model becomes distance and attractiveness alone; at 2 every
catchment's attachment doubles in the exponent, which is a very strong
map indeed. At 1 it uses the fitted values.

That single multiplier is deliberately blunt. It answers "what if
families follow their catchments more, or less, than they do now?"
without pretending to know which catchment would change.

```{r gamma-slider}
#| tbl-cap: "What the slider does to the share of children modelled at a school in their own catchment, 2026, council priorities."
purrr::map_dfr(c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2), function(g) {
  rr <- run_sim(inp, year = 2026, gamma = g, rules = list(rule = "priorities"))
  tibble(`Slider` = sprintf("%.1f×", g),
         `At a school in their own catchment` = fmt_pct(100 * rr$in_catch_share, 0))
}) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lr")
```

## Where it sits in the matrix

Unlike $O_i$ and $W_j$, the catchment term does not live in a margin. It
is a **mask over the interior**: for each neighbourhood, the cells of
schools in its own catchment are multiplied by $e^{\gamma_h}$ and the
rest are left alone.

```{r matrix-gamma}
#| tbl-cap: "The four neighbourhoods again. A cell marked with the multiplier is one where the school is in that neighbourhood's catchment; the others are untouched."
dsg <- inp$designs[["Current catchments"]]
cellmark <- function(zone, school) {
  in_c <- !is.na(dsg$school[school]) && dsg$school[school] == dsg$zone[zone]
  h <- unname(dsg$zone[zone])
  if (in_c) sprintf("$T_{ij} \\times %.1f$", exp(gam[[h]])) else "$T_{ij}$"
}
data.frame(
  Neighbourhood = c(sub("[|].*$", "", ex_zones$zone), "$W_j$"),
  `Dorothy Stringer` = c(vapply(ex_zones$zone, cellmark, "", school = sch4[1]),
                         sprintf("%.2f", W5[[sch4[1]]])),
  Varndean = c(vapply(ex_zones$zone, cellmark, "", school = sch4[2]),
               sprintf("%.2f", W5[[sch4[2]]])),
  Longhill = c(vapply(ex_zones$zone, cellmark, "", school = sch4[3]),
               sprintf("%.2f", W5[[sch4[3]]])),
  `Cardinal Newman` = c(vapply(ex_zones$zone, cellmark, "", school = sch4[4]),
                        sprintf("%.2f", W5[[sch4[4]]])),
  `$O_i$ (2026)` = c(sprintf("%.1f", ex_zones$Oi), ""),
  check.names = FALSE) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lccccr")
```

Cardinal Newman is in nobody's catchment: it and King's admit city-wide
on faith criteria, so no cell in their columns is ever multiplied. In the
two paired catchments **both** schools are in catchment, which is what
makes those catchments different objects from the four single-school
ones.

## Checks you can run

```{r gamma-checks}
#| tbl-cap: "What the catchment terms should satisfy."
prof_flat <- cal$profile %>% group_by(catchment) %>%
  summarise(span = diff(range(deviance)), .groups = "drop")
tibble::tribble(
  ~Check, ~Result,
  "Every catchment's fit has an interior minimum",
  sprintf("fitted %.1f to %.1f, grid 0 to 4", min(gam), max(gam)),
  "The data can tell one value from another",
  sprintf("deviance spans %s to %s across the grid",
          fmt_n(min(prof_flat$span)), fmt_n(max(prof_flat$span))),
  "Fitting per catchment beats one term for the city",
  sprintf("deviance %s against %s", fmt_n(cal$fit$deviance[cal$fit$model == "M5"]),
          fmt_n(cal$fit$deviance[cal$fit$model == "M4"])),
  "Modelled children at a catchment school, today",
  fmt_pct(100 * r_now$in_catch_share, 0),
  "Slider at zero removes the map entirely",
  fmt_pct(100 * run_sim(inp, year = 2026, gamma = 0,
                        rules = list(rule = "priorities"))$in_catch_share, 0)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lr")
```

## What to be careful about

::: {.callout-warning}

## The assumption every redraw result depends on

The terms are fitted on the map families have lived with, and then
**carried unchanged to any other map**. A redraw in the simulator moves
which schools count as in catchment; it does not change how strongly a
family follows the line.

That is the single most consequential assumption in this work. If
families follow a new boundary less closely than the one they know —
which the strategic view finds some evidence for in what happened after
2024 — then every redraw result here is too optimistic about how many
children the redraw moves. The strategic view reports the halved-term
version of the relocation runs for exactly this reason.
:::

- **The term is fitted on the pre-2024 map**, because that is the map the
  preference table covers.
- **It bundles several mechanisms.** Siblings already at the school, the
  free bus, habit, and the sense that the catchment school is *the*
  school all end up in one number, because the table cannot separate
  them.
- **It is a home-catchment term, not a school term.** A school in two
  catchments — none exist today, but CoMArt opening would create one —
  takes each catchment's own strength.
- **Paired catchments are a single object here.** A Stringer / Varndean
  family gets the bonus on both schools, and which of the two they prefer
  is left to $W_j$, distance, and the exclusivity populations.

## Questions this raises

1. Should the term decay when a boundary changes — a family newly placed
   in a catchment following it less closely than one that has been in it
   for years?
2. Should it vary with how many schools a catchment contains, rather than
   being one number per catchment?
3. Would first preferences by small area, before and after the 2024
   change, let the normative half of this be separated from the
   procedural half?

# $C_j$ and $\delta$: the company a school keeps {#sec-cj}

```{r cj-setup}
#| include: false
DELTA <- inp$params$delta
SIGMA <- inp$params$sigma
sch_city <- inp$schools[inp$schools$city & !(inp$schools$hypothetical %in% TRUE), ]
W_run <- setNames(sch_city$W, sch_city$name)
xy <- sch_city %>% select(name, easting, northing)
pairs_km <- tidyr::expand_grid(name = xy$name, k = xy$name) %>%
  filter(name != k) %>%
  left_join(xy, by = "name") %>%
  left_join(xy %>% rename(k = name, ke = easting, kn = northing), by = "k") %>%
  mutate(km = pmax(sqrt((easting - ke)^2 + (northing - kn)^2) / 1000, 0.1),
         Wk = unname(W_run[k]), contrib = Wk * km^-SIGMA,
         short = short_sch(name), k_short = short_sch(k))

sch_elm <- sch_city
lh_row <- sch_elm$name == "Longhill High School"
sch_elm$easting[lh_row] <- sch_city$elm_easting[lh_row]
sch_elm$northing[lh_row] <- sch_city$elm_northing[lh_row]
C_now <- compete_now(sch_city, W_run, SIGMA)
C_elm <- compete_now(sch_elm, W_run, SIGMA)

Cj <- tibble(name = names(C_now), C = unname(C_now),
             C_elm = unname(C_elm[names(C_now)])) %>%
  mutate(short = short_sch(name), index = 100 * C / mean(C),
         index_elm = 100 * C_elm / mean(C), mult = (C / mean(C))^DELTA)
cj_of <- function(s, col) Cj[[col]][Cj$short == s]
min_km <- function(s) min(pairs_km$km[pairs_km$short == s])
rmse0 <- function(x) x$rmse[abs(x$value) < 1e-8]
r2_0  <- function(x) x$r2[abs(x$value) < 1e-8]
```

## What it is

$C_j$ measures **how much company a school has**: how many other schools
stand close to it, weighted by how wanted each of them is.

$$C_j \;=\; \sum_{k \neq j} W_k\, d_{jk}^{-\sigma}, \qquad \sigma = `r sprintf("%.0f", SIGMA)`$$

$d_{jk}$ is the straight-line distance in kilometres between two
**schools**, and it deliberately carries a different symbol from
$c_{ij}$: nobody travels from one school to another, so routing it would
mean nothing. All that is wanted is a measure of how clustered the
schools are. With $\sigma$ at `r sprintf("%.0f", SIGMA)` the term reduces
to *the sum of the rivals' attractiveness per kilometre they are away*.

It enters the model as a power on the pull:

$$\text{pull} \;\propto\; W_j\, c_{ij}^{-\beta}\, e^{\gamma_{h}\mathbb{1}[\cdot]}\, C_j^{\,\delta}, \qquad \delta = `r sprintf("%+.1f", DELTA)`$$

The reasoning is Fotheringham's: a plain gravity model is misspecified
when destinations cluster, because people choose an area first and a
destination within it second. Left out, the clustering does not go away —
it is absorbed by the distance parameter instead.

## Brighton in one term

```{r fig-cj-map}
#| fig-cap: "Each school sized by the company it keeps, with its score on an index where the city average is 100. The lines open up the two extremes: every rival's contribution to Dorothy Stringer's total in orange, and to Longhill's in navy. A thicker line is a bigger contribution."
#| fig-height: 5.0
sch_pts <- sch_city %>%
  select(name, easting, northing) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("easting", "northing"), crs = 27700) %>%
  st_transform(4326) %>%
  mutate(short = short_sch(name),
         lon = st_coordinates(.)[, 1], lat = st_coordinates(.)[, 2]) %>%
  left_join(Cj %>% select(name, C, index), by = "name")
lonlat <- sch_pts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% select(name, lon, lat)
segs <- pairs_km %>%
  filter(short %in% c("Dorothy Stringer", "Longhill")) %>%
  left_join(lonlat, by = "name") %>%
  left_join(lonlat %>% rename(k = name, klon = lon, klat = lat), by = "k")

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = catch_sf, fill = "grey96", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_segment(data = segs, aes(x = lon, y = lat, xend = klon, yend = klat,
                                linewidth = contrib, colour = short), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_sf(data = sch_pts, aes(size = C), shape = 21, fill = "white",
          colour = "black", stroke = 0.9) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data = sch_pts, aes(lon, lat, label = sprintf("%s\n%.0f", short, index)),
    size = 2.9, lineheight = 0.9, colour = "#1f3b57", seed = 11,
    box.padding = 0.45, point.padding = 0.3, min.segment.length = 0.2,
    segment.colour = "grey55", segment.size = 0.3, max.overlaps = Inf) +
  scale_linewidth_continuous(range = c(0.2, 3.4), guide = "none") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(2, 9), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Dorothy Stringer` = "#d95f02", Longhill = "#1f3b57"),
                      name = NULL,
                      labels = function(x) paste("contributions to", x)) +
  coord_sf(expand = TRUE, clip = "off") +
  labs(title = "Five hundred metres from a rival, or five kilometres",
       subtitle = "The competing-destinations term by school, city average = 100") +
  theme_void(12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#1f3b57"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey35"),
        legend.position = "top")
```

The two ends of the city are different objects on this measure.

```{r cj-contrib}
#| tbl-cap: "What the term is made of at its two extremes. Each row is one rival: how far away it is, how wanted it is, and what it therefore contributes."
pairs_km %>%
  filter(short %in% c("Dorothy Stringer", "Longhill")) %>%
  group_by(short) %>% arrange(desc(contrib), .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(rank = row_number(), total = sum(contrib)) %>%
  filter(rank <= 3) %>% ungroup() %>%
  transmute(School = sprintf("%s (total %.2f)", short, total),
            Rival = k_short, `Distance (km)` = sprintf("%.2f", km),
            `Its $W_k$` = sprintf("%.2f", Wk),
            Contribution = sprintf("%.2f", contrib)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "llrrr")
```

Varndean stands `r sprintf("%.0f", 1000 * min_km("Dorothy Stringer"))`
metres from Dorothy Stringer, and Cardinal Newman — the most wanted
school in the city on $W_j$ — is under two kilometres from both. Those
two rivals alone contribute more to Stringer's term than **all nine** of
Longhill's rivals contribute to its own. On an index with the city
average at 100, Stringer scores
`r sprintf("%.0f", cj_of("Dorothy Stringer", "index"))` and Longhill
`r sprintf("%.0f", cj_of("Longhill", "index"))`.

Two features of the term follow from how it is built, and both matter in
the simulator:

- **It uses the attractiveness in force, not a fixed table.** Pull an
  attractiveness slider and every *other* school's $C_j$ moves too,
  because $W_k$ sits inside the sum.
- **It is a sum over the schools that exist in a run.** Close a school and
  its neighbours lose the company it was providing; open CoMArt in East
  Brighton and Longhill gains some.

## What the fitted exponent does

$\delta$ was fitted by grid search over
`r sprintf("%+.1f to %+.1f", min(mt$delta_fit$value), max(mt$delta_fit$value))`,
against the offers the council made in the most recent round, with the
capacity ceiling and the catchment term already in place (§6 explains why
the ceiling goes in first).

```{r fig-cj-delta}
#| fig-cap: "How much the term improves the fit, for three versions of the model. Each curve is that version's error against the offers made, relative to itself at δ = 0, so below 1 means the term is earning its place. The shaded half is the sign Fotheringham's argument predicts."
#| fig-height: 4.8
dprof <- bind_rows(
  mt$delta_fit   %>% mutate(v = "With the ceiling and the catchment term"),
  mt$delta_alone %>% mutate(v = "With the ceiling only"),
  mt$delta_nocap %>% mutate(v = "With neither")) %>%
  group_by(v) %>% mutate(rel = rmse / rmse[abs(value) < 1e-8]) %>% ungroup() %>%
  mutate(v = factor(v, c("With the ceiling and the catchment term",
                         "With the ceiling only", "With neither")))
ggplot(dprof, aes(value, rel, colour = v)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = min(dprof$value), xmax = 0, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#b2182b", alpha = 0.05) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = dprof %>% group_by(v) %>% slice_min(rel, n = 1) %>% ungroup(),
             size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  annotate("text", x = min(dprof$value) + 0.05, y = 1.55, hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
           size = 3.5, colour = "#b2182b", lineheight = 0.95,
           label = "rivals take share\n(competing destinations)") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#1f3b57", "#d95f02", "grey60"), name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.8, 1.6)) +
  labs(x = "δ", y = "Error, relative to the same model at δ = 0",
       title = sprintf("Fitted at δ = %+.1f, on the wrong side of zero", DELTA),
       subtitle = "Dots mark each version's best value") +
  theme_bh() +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.direction = "vertical",
        legend.justification = "left")
```

**The sign is not the one the term was added to test.** A negative
$\delta$ is the competing-destinations prediction: rivals nearby take
share. The fit lands at `r sprintf("%+.1f", DELTA)` — a school does
slightly *better* for having company. That is agglomeration, the pattern
of retail parks and restaurant streets, rather than the correction
Fotheringham proposed. Negative values are not marginally worse but much
worse: at $\delta = -1$ the error is about
`r sprintf("%.1f", mt$delta_fit$rmse[which.min(abs(mt$delta_fit$value + 1))] / min(mt$delta_fit$rmse))`
times its best.

Three things keep the finding modest:

- **The gain is small.** RMSE falls from
  `r sprintf("%.1f", rmse0(mt$delta_fit))` at $\delta = 0$ to
  `r sprintf("%.1f", min(mt$delta_fit$rmse))` at the fitted value, and
  $R^2$ from `r sprintf("%.3f", r2_0(mt$delta_fit))` to
  `r sprintf("%.3f", mt$delta_fit$r2[which.min(mt$delta_fit$rmse)])`.
- **Without the ceiling it does nothing at all.** Fitted with no capacity
  constraint the best value is `r sprintf("%+.1f", mt$delta_nocap_hat)`
  and the error moves only from `r sprintf("%.1f", rmse0(mt$delta_nocap))`
  to `r sprintf("%.1f", min(mt$delta_nocap$rmse))` — the grey curve above,
  which barely dips below its own starting point. What the term appears to explain is mostly rationing.
- **It and $\gamma$ are partly substitutes.** With the ceiling but no
  catchment term, $\delta$ on its own fits at
  `r sprintf("%+.1f", mt$delta_alone_hat)` and reaches much the same
  error. Both terms hand extra pull to the same central schools by
  different routes, so neither is a clean estimate of its own mechanism.

```{r cj-multiplier}
#| tbl-cap: "What the term does to each school's pull at the fitted exponent. A multiplier of 1 would be no effect. The last column is the same index with Longhill rebuilt at Elm Grove, which changes the distances every school is measured against."
Cj %>% arrange(desc(index)) %>%
  transmute(School = short,
            `$C_j$ (city average = 100)` = sprintf("%.0f", index),
            `Multiplies its pull by` = sprintf("%.2f", mult),
            `$C_j$ with Longhill at Elm Grove` = sprintf("%.0f", index_elm)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrr")
```

So the effect on pull runs from about
`r sprintf("%.2f", min(Cj$mult))` for the most isolated school to
`r sprintf("%.2f", max(Cj$mult))` for the most crowded: Longhill's pull
is cut by roughly `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (1 - min(Cj$mult)))`% against
the city average and Stringer's raised by about
`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (max(Cj$mult) - 1))`%. Smaller than $\gamma$ or
$\beta$, but not nothing.

## Why it is in the model at all

Three reasons, none of them "it improved the fit a lot":

1. **It is the standard correction** for a gravity model over clustered
   destinations. Leaving it out does not remove the clustering; it loads
   it onto $\beta$, and the distance parameter then means two things at
   once.
2. **It moves when a school moves.** Rebuilt at Elm Grove, Longhill's
   term rises from `r sprintf("%.0f", cj_of("Longhill", "index"))` to
   `r sprintf("%.0f", cj_of("Longhill", "index_elm"))` — still below
   average, but no longer alone on the eastern edge. That is a real
   difference between the two sites and the model should see it. It is
   also a correction made in this version: before it, competition was
   measured from Ovingdean even in runs where the school had moved.
3. **It records a negative finding.** That a compact city of ten schools
   shows no competing-destinations effect is worth reporting, and it is
   at least consistent with the structure: a production-constrained model
   already normalises each neighbourhood's choices across every school
   through $A_i$ (§8), which is where much of the work the term would
   otherwise do has already been done.

## Checks you can run

```{r cj-checks}
#| tbl-cap: "What the competing-destinations term should satisfy."
tibble::tribble(
  ~Check, ~Result,
  "Schools in the sum",
  sprintf("%d city schools; out-of-city destinations carry no C_j at all",
          nrow(sch_city)),
  "Distances are school to school, straight line",
  sprintf("%.2f km to %.2f km", min(pairs_km$km), max(pairs_km$km)),
  "Closest pair in the city",
  sprintf("%s and %s, %.0f m", pairs_km$short[which.min(pairs_km$km)],
          pairs_km$k_short[which.min(pairs_km$km)], 1000 * min(pairs_km$km)),
  "Most isolated school",
  sprintf("%s, nearest rival %.1f km", Cj$short[which.min(Cj$C)],
          min_km(Cj$short[which.min(Cj$C)])),
  "Rivals are attractiveness-weighted",
  "yes: an unwanted neighbour counts for less than a wanted one",
  "Effect on pull at the fitted exponent",
  sprintf("%.2f to %.2f times", min(Cj$mult), max(Cj$mult)),
  "Measured from where each school stands in the run",
  sprintf("yes: Longhill scores %.0f at Ovingdean and %.0f at Elm Grove",
          cj_of("Longhill", "index"), cj_of("Longhill", "index_elm"))) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lr")
```

## What to be careful about

- **$\sigma$ is set, not fitted.** The decay on school-to-school distance
  is fixed at `r sprintf("%.0f", SIGMA)`. Fitting it as well as $\delta$
  on ten destination margins would be asking too much of the data.
- **Ten schools.** Every statement here rests on ten points, and two
  tight pairs — Stringer with Varndean, Blatchington Mill with Hove Park
  — dominate the variation.
- **It is entangled with $W_j$ and with $\gamma$.** The sum uses the
  attractiveness that was itself balanced with this term in place, and
  §6's catchment term can do much of the same work.
- **Straight lines, not journeys.** Two schools half a kilometre apart
  across a railway are as close, on this measure, as two half a kilometre
  apart on the same street.
- **Fitted on offers, not preferences.** Unlike $\gamma_h$, which was
  refitted against the catchment preference table, $\delta$ was fitted
  against the offers made — and those are shaped by the ceiling as much
  as by choice.

## Questions this raises

1. Should $\delta$ be refitted against preferences, as $\gamma_h$ now is?
   That is the cleaner question, and this is the last term still fitted
   against the older target.
2. Is the positive sign real, or is it standing in for something the
   model is missing — the faith schools' city-wide draw, say, which
   happens to sit in the crowded middle of the city?
3. Would a nested form — choose an area, then a school within it —
   represent the paired catchments better than an exponent on clustering
   does?

# $A_i$: the balancing factor {#sec-ai}

```{r ai-setup}
#| include: false
r_ai <- run_sim(inp, year = 2026, rules = list(rule = "priorities"))
d_ai <- r_ai$flows
ext_ai <- inp$params$outside
g_ai <- unname(inp$params$gamma[d_ai$catchment]); g_ai[is.na(g_ai)] <- 0
d_ai$util <- d_ai$Wj * d_ai$cij^(-inp$params$beta) *
  exp(g_ai * d_ai$in_catch + inp$params$delta * log(d_ai$Cj))
is_ext <- d_ai$name %in% names(ext_ai$W)
d_ai$util[is_ext] <- unname(ext_ai$W[d_ai$name[is_ext]]) *
  d_ai$km[is_ext]^(-ext_ai$decay)

# The engine's own answer, to check the hand computation against.
own <- tapply(d_ai$util, d_ai$orig, sum)
d_ai$A <- 1 / own[d_ai$orig]
d_ai$by_hand <- d_ai$util * d_ai$Oi_pop * d_ai$A
ai_gap <- max(abs(d_ai$by_hand - d_ai$wanted))

pull_z <- d_ai %>% filter(pop == "either") %>%
  group_by(zone) %>%
  summarise(pull = sum(util), Oi = first(Oi_pop), catchment = first(catchment),
            ext_share = sum(util[name %in% names(ext_ai$W)]) / sum(util),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(A = 1 / pull, index = 100 * pull / stats::median(pull))

row_chk <- d_ai %>% group_by(orig) %>%
  summarise(Oi = first(Oi_pop), wanted = sum(wanted), final = sum(flow), .groups = "drop")

ZC <- "E01016901|DS_Varndean|DS_Varndean"
ZE <- "E01017012|Longhill|Longhill"
worked <- function(zz) d_ai %>% filter(zone == zz, pop == "either")
ai_tbl <- function(zz) {
  worked(zz) %>%
    transmute(School = short_sch(name), `Journey (min)` = sprintf("%.0f", cij),
              `$W_j$` = ifelse(is.na(Wj), "—", sprintf("%.2f", Wj)),
              `In catchment` = ifelse(in_catch == 1, "yes", ""),
              Pull = signif(util, 3),
              `Share of the row` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * util / sum(util)),
              Children = sprintf("%.1f", wanted)) %>%
    arrange(desc(Pull)) %>%
    mutate(Pull = format(Pull, scientific = TRUE, digits = 3)) %>%
    head(6)
}
ai_of <- function(zz) 1 / sum(worked(zz)$util)
oi_of <- function(zz) worked(zz)$Oi_pop[1]
```

## What it is

$A_i$ is not a thing anyone chooses or observes. It is whatever number
makes each neighbourhood's row of the matrix add up to the children who
live there:

$$\sum_j T_{ij}^{\,y} = O_i^{\,y} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
A_i^{\,y} \;=\; \frac{1}{\sum_k W_k\, c_{ik}^{-\beta}\,
e^{\gamma_{h(i)}\mathbb{1}[\cdot]}\, C_k^{\delta}}$$

Call the denominator the neighbourhood's **total pull**: everything the
city offers it, discounted by how hard each school is to reach. $A_i$ is
its reciprocal, and the model then divides the children of $i$ between
schools in proportion to each school's share of that total:

$$T_{ij} \;=\; O_i \times \frac{\text{pull}_{ij}}{\sum_k \text{pull}_{ik}}$$

This is what "production-constrained" means, and it is the single
strongest assumption in the model. **Every child is placed somewhere.**
Demand cannot leak away, and it cannot grow because the city got better:
if every school became less attractive tomorrow, $A_i$ would simply rise
to compensate and exactly the same children would be distributed in
exactly the same proportions.

## Computed per population, not per zone

One subtlety: the model does not balance over zones but over
**origin-populations**. In the two paired catchments some families will
take one of the pair but not the other, so a zone there carries up to
three populations with different choice sets, each balanced on its own.

```{r ai-pops}
#| tbl-cap: "The origin-populations the model balances over. Each is a group of children with its own choice set, and therefore its own balancing factor."
d_ai %>% distinct(orig, pop, zone) %>%
  count(pop, name = "Origins") %>%
  mutate(Population = ifelse(pop == "either", "Everyone else", pop)) %>%
  select(Population, Origins) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lr")
```

That is `r fmt_n(nrow(row_chk))` origins over
`r fmt_n(n_distinct(d_ai$zone))` zones, and it matters because a child
who would not take Varndean must have Varndean *out of the denominator*,
not merely low in it. Otherwise refusing them at Dorothy Stringer would
send them next door.

## What the total pull looks like

```{r fig-ai-map}
#| fig-cap: "The denominator of the balancing factor: how much school, weighted by how reachable it is, each neighbourhood has available. Drawn on a log scale, because the range is more than eightyfold. Zone values are carried up to LSOAs, weighted by children."
#| fig-height: 5
pull_map <- lsoa_sf %>%
  inner_join(pull_z %>% inner_join(zone_lsoa %>% select(zone, lsoa), by = "zone") %>%
               group_by(lsoa) %>%
               summarise(index = weighted.mean(index, Oi), .groups = "drop"),
             by = c("lsoa21cd" = "lsoa"))
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = pull_map, aes(fill = index), colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = catch_sf, fill = NA, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = sch_sf, shape = 21, fill = "white", colour = "black",
          size = 2.4, stroke = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis", trans = "log10",
                       name = "Total pull\n(median = 100)",
                       breaks = c(30, 100, 300, 1000)) +
  labs(title = "What each neighbourhood has within reach",
       subtitle = "The sum the balancing factor divides by, current catchment map, 2026") +
  theme_void(12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#1f3b57"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey35"))
```

The range is extreme — from
`r sprintf("%.0f", min(pull_z$index))` to
`r sprintf("%.0f", max(pull_z$index))` on an index with the median at 100
— and most of it is the catchment term compounding with distance. A
neighbourhood between Dorothy Stringer and Varndean has two schools it
can walk to *and* the catchment bonus on both. A neighbourhood in
Ovingdean has one school within easy reach, with the lowest $W_j$ in the
city.

For the far east of the city the denominator also contains schools
outside it. In a typical Longhill-catchment neighbourhood they are
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * weighted.mean(pull_z$ext_share[pull_z$catchment == "Longhill"], pull_z$Oi[pull_z$catchment == "Longhill"]))`
of the total pull, and they are under
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * max(pull_z$ext_share[!pull_z$catchment %in% c("Longhill", "BACA")]))`
everywhere west of Brighton Aldridge's.

## Two rows, worked

```{r ai-worked-central}
#| tbl-cap: "A neighbourhood between the two Fiveways schools. Top six destinations of fourteen; the rest are rounding."
ai_tbl(ZC) %>% knitr::kable(align = "lrrlrrr")
```

`r sprintf("%.0f", oi_of(ZC))` children, total pull
`r sprintf("%.3f", 1 / ai_of(ZC))`, so
$A_i = `r sprintf("%.2f", ai_of(ZC))`$.

```{r ai-worked-east}
#| tbl-cap: "A neighbourhood in Longhill's catchment. The same table, the same city, a different world."
ai_tbl(ZE) %>% knitr::kable(align = "lrrlrrr")
```

`r sprintf("%.0f", oi_of(ZE))` children, total pull
`r sprintf("%.4f", 1 / ai_of(ZE))`, so
$A_i = `r sprintf("%.1f", ai_of(ZE))`$ — about
`r sprintf("%.0f", ai_of(ZE) / ai_of(ZC))` times the first.

Read the two tables side by side and the model's behaviour is visible in
one page. In the first, `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * sum(worked(ZC)$util[worked(ZC)$in_catch == 1]) / sum(worked(ZC)$util))`
of the row goes to the two catchment schools before anything else is
considered. In the second, the catchment school takes
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * sum(worked(ZE)$util[worked(ZE)$in_catch == 1]) / sum(worked(ZE)$util))`,
and the second destination is Priory School in Lewes, outside the city
altogether.

::: {.callout-note}

## The balancing factor is not the accessibility index, but it is close

The strategic view reports an accessibility index for each
neighbourhood. That is the same sum with the behavioural terms stripped
out — attractiveness and journey time only, no catchment bonus, no
competition term, city schools alone. The two rank neighbourhoods
similarly but not identically (Spearman
$\rho = `r sprintf("%.2f", cor(pull_z$pull, acc$zone$A_hansen[match(pull_z$zone, acc$zone$zone)], method = "spearman"))`$),
and the difference is mostly the catchment term: it rewards the
neighbourhoods that are already close to a wanted school.
:::

## Where it sits in the sequence

$A_i$ is applied to the **uncapped** pull, before any admission number is
consulted. The model first works out what families want, and only then
rations it (§9), re-offering the children who are refused (§10).

The constraint survives that. After the ceiling and the re-offering, the
row still sums to the children who live there — nobody is lost in
rationing, they are only placed elsewhere:

```{r ai-checks}
#| tbl-cap: "What the balancing factor should satisfy. Every number here is computed from the run, not asserted."
tibble::tribble(
  ~Check, ~Result,
  "Origins balanced",
  sprintf("%s populations over %s zones", fmt_n(nrow(row_chk)),
          fmt_n(n_distinct(d_ai$zone))),
  "Rows sum to their children, before the ceiling",
  sprintf("largest error %.0e children", max(abs(row_chk$wanted - row_chk$Oi))),
  "Rows still sum to their children, after it",
  sprintf("largest error %.2f children", max(abs(row_chk$final - row_chk$Oi))),
  "City total placed",
  sprintf("%s children in 2026, all of them", fmt_n(round(sum(d_ai$flow)))),
  "Recomputing the flows by hand reproduces the engine",
  sprintf("largest difference %.0e children", ai_gap),
  "Range of the balancing factor",
  sprintf("%.2f to %.1f", min(pull_z$A), max(pull_z$A)),
  "Out-of-city schools are inside the denominator",
  "yes: they compete for children like any other destination") %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lr")
```

## What to be careful about

- **No demand response.** Because the row is fixed at $O_i$, nothing the
  model does can make families leave the state system, home-school, move
  house, or appear from elsewhere. A scenario that makes every school
  worse produces the same `r fmt_n(round(sum(d_ai$flow)))` placements as
  one that makes every school better. Where a scenario would plausibly change how many families opt
  out, the model will not show it, and §2's state-sector share is the
  only place that quantity lives.
- **Substitution is proportional.** Close a school, and the children who
  wanted it are redistributed among the others in proportion to those
  schools' existing pull for that neighbourhood — the classic
  independence-of-irrelevant-alternatives behaviour. The exclusivity
  populations are a patch on exactly this, for the one case where it is
  known to be wrong.
- **It absorbs everything the model does not contain.** Any systematic
  pull the equation misses is silently rescaled away by $A_i$ rather than
  showing up as a residual. A model that fits well at the school level
  can still be wrong about why.
- **It is recomputed in every run.** Change a year, a slider, a boundary
  or a school's existence and the denominator changes for every affected
  neighbourhood. $A_i$ is never carried over between runs.

## Questions this raises

1. Should the state-sector share respond to the scenario rather than
   being fixed in $O_i$ — a doubly-constrained or elastic form?
2. Should the choice set be truncated — some neighbourhoods carry
   fourteen destinations when families realistically consider three or
   four?
3. Are the exclusivity populations the right patch for proportional
   substitution, or should the whole thing be nested?

# The admission-number ceiling {#sec-cap}

```{r cap-setup}
#| include: false
rl <- inp$rules
r_pri <- r_ai                         # priorities ceiling, from §8
r_pub <- run_sim(inp, year = 2026)    # the proportional ceiling
r_free <- run_sim(inp, year = 2026, capped = FALSE)

by_sch <- r_pri$flows %>%
  group_by(name) %>%
  summarise(wanted = sum(wanted), offered = sum(flow), .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(inp$schools %>% select(name, pan, city, faith), by = "name") %>%
  filter(city) %>%
  mutate(short = short_sch(name),
         community = name %in% rl$community,
         over = wanted - pan)

excess <- sum(pmax(by_sch$over, 0))
at_pan <- sum(by_sch$offered >= by_sch$pan - 0.5)

tier_obs <- rl$outturn_2026 %>%
  mutate(tier = dplyr::case_when(priority %in% 4:5 ~ "FSM (4, 5)",
                                 priority == 6 ~ "Single-school catchment (6)",
                                 priority %in% c(3, 7) ~ "In catchment, siblings included (3, 7)",
                                 priority == 8 ~ "Everyone else (8)",
                                 TRUE ~ "Looked-after, SEN, exceptional (0-2)")) %>%
  group_by(School = short_sch(school), tier) %>%
  summarise(observed = sum(offers), .groups = "drop")

tier_mod <- r_pri$tiers %>%
  filter(name %in% rl$rationing) %>%
  transmute(School = short_sch(name),
            `FSM (4, 5)` = p45_in + p45_out,
            `Single-school catchment (6)` = p6,
            `In catchment, siblings included (3, 7)` = p7,
            `Everyone else (8)` = p8) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-School, names_to = "tier", values_to = "modelled")

tier_cmp <- tier_mod %>% left_join(tier_obs, by = c("School", "tier"))
unmodelled <- tier_obs %>% filter(tier == "Looked-after, SEN, exceptional (0-2)")

# Tiers against each school's own admission number and modelled intake.
tier_pan <- r_pri$tiers %>%
  left_join(inp$schools %>% select(name, pan), by = "name") %>%
  left_join(r_pri$flows %>% group_by(name) %>%
              summarise(intake = sum(flow), .groups = "drop"), by = "name") %>%
  mutate(fsm_share = (p45_in + p45_out) / pan, p6_share = p6 / pan) %>%
  select(name, p45_in, p45_out, p6, p7, p8, pan, intake, fsm_share, p6_share)
tier_pan <- tier_pan %>% select(name, p45_in, p45_out, p6, p7, p8, intake,
                                fsm_share, p6_share)
```

## What happens after the matrix

Sections 2 to 8 produce $T_{ij}$: how many children in each neighbourhood
**want** each school as their first choice. Nothing in that calculation
knows how many places a school has. The city's demand, laid against the
admission numbers and against what families actually named, does not
fit:

```{r fig-cap-demand}
#| fig-cap: "Each school's places against how many families ask for it. The model's demand is a first choice. The published counts show how many families named the school first, and first or second, in the 2026 round. Under the council's equal-preference system every one of those preferences can win a place."
#| fig-height: 5.6
pair_either <- d_ai %>%
  filter(pop == "either", catchment == "DS_Varndean", name == "Varndean School") %>%
  summarise(Varndean = sum(wanted))
prefs26 <- bh_data("factsheet_panel.rds")$factsheets %>%
  filter(year == 2026, name != "Total") %>%
  transmute(name, pref1, pref12 = pref1 + pref2, off1)
dem <- by_sch %>%
  left_join(prefs26, by = "name") %>%
  mutate(short = forcats::fct_reorder(short, pan))
dem_long <- dem %>%
  select(short, `Model: first choice` = wanted,
         `Named first (published)` = pref1,
         `Named first or second (published)` = pref12,
         `Offered, model` = offered) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-short, names_to = "what", values_to = "n") %>%
  mutate(what = factor(what, c("Model: first choice", "Named first (published)",
                               "Named first or second (published)", "Offered, model")))
ggplot(dem_long, aes(n, short)) +
  geom_segment(data = dem, aes(x = 0, xend = pan, y = short, yend = short),
               colour = "grey86", linewidth = 7) +
  geom_segment(data = dem, aes(x = pref1, xend = pref12, y = short, yend = short),
               colour = "#d95f02", alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = what, shape = what), size = 3.2) +
  geom_text(data = dem, aes(x = 0, label = sprintf("%d places ", pan)),
            hjust = 1, size = 2.9, colour = "grey40") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#d95f02", "#9e6a3b", "#d95f02", "#1f3b57"), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(17, 1, 16, 15), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.14, 0.03))) +
  labs(x = "Children or families, 2026", y = NULL,
       title = sprintf("Counting second choices, %d of the ten schools are over-asked",
                       sum(dem$pref12 > dem$pan)),
       subtitle = "Grey bar: the admission number. Named counts: council factsheet, 2026.") +
  theme_bh() +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.direction = "horizontal",
        plot.title.position = "plot") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2), shape = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

**The model's demand is a first choice, and a first choice is not the
whole story.** The council runs an equal-preference system: every school
a family names is considered on the same footing, and a family is offered
the highest-ranked of its schools where it qualifies. So a school can be
named first by fewer families than it holds and still refuse some of
them. Dorothy Stringer is the clearest case. In 2026
`r fmt_n(dem$pref1[dem$short == "Dorothy Stringer"])` families put it
first, against `r dem$pan[dem$short == "Dorothy Stringer"]` places, and
`r fmt_n(dem$pref12[dem$short == "Dorothy Stringer"] - dem$pref1[dem$short == "Dorothy Stringer"])`
more put it second. Only `r dem$off1[dem$short == "Dorothy Stringer"]`
of those who put it first were offered it: the rest of its places went to
families with a higher priority who had ranked it second or third.

The model represents that in two places rather than in the demand
itself. Families in the two paired catchments are treated as content with
either school unless they are among the few who would take only one
(`r fmt_pct(100 * inp$params$exclusive$share[inp$params$exclusive$school == "Dorothy Stringer School"])`
would take only Stringer and
`r fmt_pct(100 * inp$params$exclusive$share[inp$params$exclusive$school == "Varndean School"])`
only Varndean, §8), and a family refused at one school of a pair is
offered the other before anywhere else (§10). Counting those families,
the model's demand for Stringer as a first choice *or* as the partner of
a first choice at Varndean is
`r fmt_n(round(dem$wanted[dem$short == "Dorothy Stringer"] + pair_either$Varndean))`,
against the `r fmt_n(dem$pref12[dem$short == "Dorothy Stringer"])`
families who named it first or second.

The ceiling is where the model stops being about preferences and starts
being about administration. It is also where most of the fit comes from:
§7 showed that without it the behavioural terms explain almost nothing.

## Two ceilings

The simulator carries both, and which one is in force is a setting.

**The proportional ceiling** (`rule = "published"`) cuts every applicant
to an oversubscribed school back by the same share. That is the average
outcome of a single lottery over everyone who applied, and it is what the
published model used before the council's priorities were added.

**The tiered ceiling** (`rule = "priorities"`) fills each community
school's places in the council's own order, and runs a proportional cut
only *within* a tier — which is what a lottery inside a priority averages
to. Every number in this guide and in the strategic view uses this one.

```{r cap-tiers}
#| tbl-cap: "The council's oversubscription priorities as the model applies them at the six community schools. Academies and faith schools keep the proportional ceiling: their criteria are not in any published data."
tibble::tribble(
  ~Priority, ~`Who`, ~`Ceiling on the tier`,
  "1–3", "Looked-after children, SEN and exceptional need, siblings",
  "not separable in zone-level flows — see below",
  "4", "Children eligible for free school meals living in the catchment",
  sprintf("with 5, up to %.0f%% of the admission number", 100 * rl$fsm_cap_share),
  "5", "Children eligible for free school meals living elsewhere",
  sprintf("with 4, up to %.0f%% of the admission number", 100 * rl$fsm_cap_share),
  "6", "Children from a single-school catchment applying outside it",
  sprintf("up to %.0f%% of the admission number", 100 * rl$p6_share),
  "7", "Children living in the catchment", "whatever is left",
  "8", "Everyone else", "whatever is left after that") %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lll")
```

A child who misses a capped tier drops to the one below: an FSM child in
the catchment falls to 7, an FSM child from elsewhere to 6 if they
qualify and 8 if not, a priority-6 child to 8. Nobody is removed from the
queue by missing a tier.

::: {.callout-note}

## What the model cannot see: priorities 1 to 3

Looked-after children, children with SEN or exceptional need, and
siblings cannot be told apart in flows between neighbourhoods and
schools — nothing in the published data says which children have a
sibling already at a school. Most siblings live in the catchment, so
they sit inside tier 7, and the comparison below folds the council's
published priority 3 into tier 7 for that reason.

The tie-break *inside* each priority is a random draw, not distance: the
council's published admission arrangements break ties by random
allocation. That is what makes a proportional cut within a tier the right
average.
:::

## Who counts as FSM

The tiers need to know how many children in each neighbourhood are
eligible for free school meals. The model has no pupil records, so it
uses the neighbourhood's IDACI score scaled by a single number:

$$\text{FSM share of zone } i \;=\; \min\!\left(`r sprintf("%.2f", rl$fsm_takeup)` \times \text{IDACI}_i,\; 0.95\right)$$

That multiplier is not chosen. It is solved for, so that the FSM-priority
places the model gives at the three rationing schools total the
`r sum(rl$outturn_2026$offers[rl$outturn_2026$priority %in% 4:5])`
the council actually made in 2026. It puts
`r fmt_pct(100 * rl$fsm_city)` of the city's Year 7 children in the FSM
group. It is a *calibrated* quantity, not a measured one, and it inherits
whatever IDACI gets wrong about who is eligible where.

## Against the published outturn

The council publishes, for the three schools that actually rationed in
2026, how many offers went out under each priority. The model was fitted
to the total of tiers 4 and 5 only; everything else in this chart is free.

```{r fig-cap-tiers}
#| fig-cap: "Offers by priority at the three schools that rationed in 2026: what the council published, and what the model produces. Only the FSM total across the three schools was calibrated; the rest is the model's own."
#| fig-height: 5
tier_cmp %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(modelled, observed), names_to = "src", values_to = "n") %>%
  mutate(src = factor(src, c("observed", "modelled"), c("Council", "Model")),
         tier = factor(tier, c("FSM (4, 5)", "Single-school catchment (6)",
                               "In catchment, siblings included (3, 7)",
                               "Everyone else (8)"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(n, forcats::fct_rev(tier), fill = src)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.65) +
  facet_wrap(~ School, ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Council = "#1f3b57", Model = "#d95f02"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Offers", y = NULL,
       title = "The ceiling, tier by tier, against what the council did",
       subtitle = "2026 entry. The council's priorities 0 to 2 are left out; the model cannot separate them from the tiers it has") +
  theme_bh() +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0))
```

The catchment tier is close at all three schools, and priority 6 is
almost exact — it is capped at
`r fmt_pct(100 * rl$p6_share)` of the admission number and the model
fills the cap, as the council did. The FSM tiers are the weak point: the
model gives Varndean the full
`r fmt_pct(100 * rl$fsm_cap_share)` and the council gave it fewer,
because an FSM child with a sibling at the school is admitted under
priority 3 and never reaches the FSM tier at all. The three-school total
is right by construction; the split between them is the model's own, and
it is too generous where siblings are most common.

`r fmt_n(sum(unmodelled$observed))` offers across the three schools went
to looked-after children, children with SEN and exceptional need. The
model places those children somewhere — it just cannot tell you that
this is why.

## What the ceiling does to the city

```{r cap-effect}
#| tbl-cap: "The two ceilings compared. A school can end up fuller than its own demand: that is the re-offering of children refused elsewhere, which is the next section."
by_sch %>%
  left_join(r_pub$flows %>% group_by(name) %>%
              summarise(pub = sum(flow), .groups = "drop"), by = "name") %>%
  arrange(desc(wanted)) %>%
  transmute(School = short, Places = pan,
            `Wanted` = sprintf("%.0f", wanted),
            `Proportional ceiling` = sprintf("%.0f", pub),
            `Council's priorities` = sprintf("%.0f", offered)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrr")
```

`r at_pan` of the `r nrow(by_sch)` city schools fill. The two at the
bottom of the table are the mirror image: Longhill is offered
`r sprintf("%.0f", by_sch$offered[by_sch$short == "Longhill"])` children
against `r by_sch$pan[by_sch$short == "Longhill"]` places, and no ceiling
anywhere in the city changes that.

Notice Dorothy Stringer and Blatchington Mill. Both are the *first*
choice of fewer children than they have places for, and both finish
full. The places are taken by children whose first choice was full ---
at Varndean, Cardinal Newman and King's --- and for whom these schools
were the partner or the second preference. That is the subject of §10,
and it is why the published counts above, which include second
preferences, show both schools heavily asked for.

## Checks you can run

```{r cap-checks}
#| tbl-cap: "What the ceiling should satisfy."
tibble::tribble(
  ~Check, ~Result,
  "No school exceeds its admission number",
  sprintf("largest overshoot %.2f children", max(by_sch$offered - by_sch$pan)),
  "Every tiered school's tiers sum to its intake",
  sprintf("largest error %.2f children",
          max(abs(rowSums(tier_pan[, 2:6]) - tier_pan$intake))),
  "The FSM tiers never exceed their cap",
  sprintf("largest use %.1f%% of the admission number, at %s",
          100 * max(tier_pan$fsm_share),
          short_sch(tier_pan$name[which.max(tier_pan$fsm_share)])),
  "Priority 6 never exceeds its cap",
  sprintf("largest use %.1f%% of the admission number",
          100 * max(tier_pan$p6_share)),
  "FSM offers at the three rationing schools",
  sprintf("%.0f modelled against %d published",
          sum((r_pri$tiers$p45_in + r_pri$tiers$p45_out)[r_pri$tiers$name %in% rl$rationing]),
          sum(rl$outturn_2026$offers[rl$outturn_2026$priority %in% 4:5])),
  "Children are not lost at the ceiling",
  sprintf("%s placed with it, %s without",
          fmt_n(round(sum(r_pri$flows$flow))), fmt_n(round(sum(r_free$flows$flow))))) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lr")
```

## What to be careful about

- **It is a mean, not a draw.** Every number here is the average outcome
  of the lottery, so no scenario in this work shows the spread. The
  variance of a real allocation round is not modelled.
- **Admission numbers are the published ones**, not the numbers a school
  could take. Where a school has taken over its admission number in the
  past, the model will not.
- **Only community schools get the tiers.** The two academy trusts and
  the two faith schools keep the proportional cut, so their intakes carry
  no priority structure at all — and Cardinal Newman has the largest
  admission number in the city.
- **The FSM group is a neighbourhood share, not a child.** A zone
  contributes its IDACI-scaled fraction to the FSM tiers of every school
  it sends children to. That is a reasonable average and a poor
  description of any individual.
- **Siblings are inside the catchment tier**, which makes the FSM tiers
  too large at the schools where siblings are most numerous.

## Questions this raises

1. Would a sibling term be estimable from the published data — last
   year's intake by catchment, scaled by an average family size?
2. Should the model run the lottery rather than average it, so the
   uncertainty in a marginal neighbourhood's outcome is visible?
3. Should the academies' and faith schools' own criteria be modelled from
   their published admission policies rather than left proportional?

# Re-offering the children who are refused {#sec-overflow}

```{r ov-setup}
#| include: false
# The cascade, re-run here with bookkeeping so the guide can say where
# each refused child goes. The arithmetic is ipf_priorities() line for
# line; the only additions are the tables of movements, and the final
# flows are checked against the engine's below.
kern <- inp$params$overflow
cap_ov <- setNames(as.numeric(inp$schools$pan), inp$schools$name)
ext_ov <- names(inp$params$outside$W)
cap_all_ov <- c(cap_ov[!is.na(cap_ov)],
                setNames(rep(1e6, length(ext_ov)), ext_ov))
dsg_ov <- inp$designs[["Current catchments"]]
o_pop_ov <- tapply(d_ai$Oi_pop, d_ai$orig, function(x) x[1])
fsm_z <- setNames(inp$zones$fsm, inp$zones$zone)
share_ov <- setNames(unname(fsm_z[sub("#.*$", "", names(o_pop_ov))]),
                     names(o_pop_ov))
grp_ov <- dsg_ov$school[inp$schools$name[inp$schools$city & !inp$schools$faith]]
single_ov <- names(table(grp_ov[!is.na(grp_ov)]))[table(grp_ov[!is.na(grp_ov)]) == 1]
in_c_ov <- d_ai$in_catch == 1
s6_ov <- unname(dsg_ov$zone[d_ai$zone]) %in% single_ov & !in_c_ov
com_ov <- d_ai$name %in% rl$community
partner_ov <- partner_map(inp$params$exclusive)
st_ov <- overflow_setup(d_ai$wanted, d_ai$orig, d_ai$name, d_ai$catchment,
                        d_ai$pop, kern, partner_ov)

attribute <- function(refused, room, st, name) {
  to_p <- st$pr; to_p[st$pr] <- room[st$p_idx[st$pr]]
  out <- list()
  if (any(to_p))
    out$partner <- tibble(from = name[to_p], to = name[st$p_idx[to_p]],
                          n = refused[to_p], route = "Partner school")
  rest <- refused; rest[to_p] <- 0
  w <- st$bw * room; ws <- rowsum(w, st$oid)[st$oid, 1]
  w2 <- st$u * room; ws2 <- rowsum(w2, st$oid)[st$oid, 1]
  share <- ifelse(ws > 0, w / ws, ifelse(ws2 > 0, w2 / ws2, 0))
  fr <- tibble(oid = st$oid, from = name, n = rest) %>% filter(n > 0)
  to <- tibble(oid = st$oid, to = name, s = share) %>% filter(s > 0)
  out$kernel <- fr %>%
    inner_join(to, by = "oid", relationship = "many-to-many") %>%
    transmute(from, to, n = n * s, route = "Second preferences")
  bind_rows(out)
}

ffv <- d_ai$wanted * unname(share_ov[d_ai$orig]); fnv <- d_ai$wanted - ffv
ov_att <- list(); ov_rounds <- c()
for (it in 1:500) {
  acc <- tier_accept(ffv, fnv, d_ai$name, cap_all_ov, cap_all_ov,
                     in_c_ov, s6_ov, com_ov, rl$p6_share, rl$fsm_cap_share)
  Hf <- ffv * acc$f; Hn <- fnv * acc$n; rf <- ffv - Hf; rn <- fnv - Hn
  ov_rounds <- c(ov_rounds, sum(rf + rn))
  if (sum(rf + rn) <= 1e-6) { ffv <- Hf; fnv <- Hn; break }
  room <- overflow_room(Hf + Hn, d_ai$name, cap_all_ov)
  if (!any(room)) { ffv <- Hf; fnv <- Hn; break }
  ov_att[[it]] <- attribute(rf + rn, room, st_ov, d_ai$name) %>% mutate(round = it)
  ffv <- Hf + overflow_add(rf, room, st_ov)
  fnv <- Hn + overflow_add(rn, room, st_ov)
}
ov_gap <- max(abs((ffv + fnv) - d_ai$flow))
A_ov <- bind_rows(ov_att)
by_route <- A_ov %>% group_by(route) %>% summarise(n = sum(n), .groups = "drop")
route_n <- function(r) by_route$n[by_route$route == r]

kern_tbl <- tibble(key = names(kern), share = unname(kern)) %>%
  tidyr::separate(key, c("catchment", "school"), sep = " ", extra = "merge")

```

## Why a proportional cut is not enough

The ceiling in §9 tells each full school how many of its applicants it
can take. It does not say what happens to the rest. Left there, the
production constraint of §8 would rescale each neighbourhood's remaining
flows to place its children — which spreads a child refused at Varndean
across *every* other school in proportion to how much they wanted each
one first.

That is not what happens. A family refused at Varndean who would also
take Dorothy Stringer gets Dorothy Stringer. A family refused at Cardinal
Newman goes where families in their part of the city put their second
preference. So refused demand is re-offered explicitly, in two steps, and
only ever to schools that still have room.

## Step one: the partner school

In the two paired catchments — Stringer with Varndean, Hove Park with
Blatchington Mill — a family who would take either school and is refused
at one is offered the other before anything else is considered.

```{r ov-partner}
#| tbl-cap: "The partner map. It follows the family's own catchment, so it holds under any boundary design."
tibble(key = names(partner_ov), partner = unname(partner_ov)) %>%
  tidyr::separate(key, c("Catchment", "Refused at"), sep = " ", extra = "merge") %>%
  transmute(Catchment = catch_lab(Catchment),
            `Refused at` = short_sch(`Refused at`),
            `Offered instead` = short_sch(partner)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lll")
```

The families who would take **only** one of the pair are excluded from
this step: they are carried as populations of their own (§8), and a child
who would not take Stringer is never sent there.

## Step two: the second preferences of their catchment

Everything else is shared among the schools with room, in proportion to
the **second preferences families in that home catchment actually gave**.
That is the council's catchment preference table, pooled over
`r length(cal$rounds)` rounds, normalised within each catchment:

```{r ov-kernel}
#| tbl-cap: "The three schools each catchment's families most often name second. Sixty numbers in all — six catchments by ten schools."
kern_tbl %>%
  group_by(catchment) %>% slice_max(share, n = 3) %>% ungroup() %>%
  transmute(Catchment = catch_lab(catchment),
            School = short_sch(school),
            `Share of the catchment's second preferences` = fmt_pct(100 * share)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "llr")
```

A catchment-level table would send every neighbourhood in Longhill's
catchment the same way, so it is modulated by where the neighbourhood
actually is. Each neighbourhood's weight on school $j$ is

$$b_{ij} \;=\; k_{h(i),j} \times \frac{u_{ij}}{\bar u_{h(i),j}}$$

where $u_{ij}$ is the share of $i$'s children the model sent to $j$
before rationing and $\bar u$ is the average of that share across the
catchment. A neighbourhood at the Patcham end of Varndean's catchment
therefore sends more of its overflow to Patcham than one at the other
end, without anyone having to write that rule down.

::: {.callout-note}

## When a school has moved

The second preferences in the table were given with the schools where
they stand today. If a run moves one — Longhill to Elm Grove — the
comparison $u/\bar u$ is made against the flows *at today's sites*, so a
catchment that the move brings a school nearer to sends it more of its
overflow. Without that correction the kernel would be read against a
city the families answering it never saw. With no move, the two are the
same flow and nothing changes.
:::

## What it does in 2026

```{r fig-ov-flows}
#| fig-cap: "Where refused children are re-offered, over all rounds of the cascade. The partner route is the paired catchments; everything else follows the home catchment's second preferences."
#| fig-height: 5.2
flows_plot <- A_ov %>%
  group_by(from = short_sch(from), to = short_sch(to), route) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(n), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(n > 0.5) %>%
  mutate(from = forcats::fct_reorder(from, n, sum),
         to = forcats::fct_reorder(to, n, sum))
ggplot(flows_plot, aes(n, from, fill = to)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ route, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = "Offered instead") +
  labs(x = "Children", y = "Refused at",
       title = sprintf("%.0f children are re-offered somewhere else",
                       sum(A_ov$n)),
       subtitle = sprintf("2026 entry, current catchment map. %.0f take the partner school, %.0f follow second preferences",
                          route_n("Partner school"), route_n("Second preferences"))) +
  theme_bh() +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0))
```

The cascade runs `r length(ov_rounds)` rounds, refusing
`r paste(sprintf("%.0f", head(ov_rounds, length(ov_rounds) - 1)), collapse = ", then ")`,
then nobody. Re-offered demand can overfill a school with a little
room left, so the next round cuts it back and re-offers the excess again;
the totals fall away quickly because each round has less to place and
fewer schools to place it in.

Two things in that chart are worth stating plainly. The largest single
movement in the city is **Varndean to Dorothy Stringer**
(`r sprintf("%.0f", sum(A_ov$n[short_sch(A_ov$from) == "Varndean" & short_sch(A_ov$to) == "Dorothy Stringer"]))`
children by both routes together), which is why Stringer finishes full
despite being wanted first by fewer children than it has places for. And
the schools receiving the overflow are, in order,
`r paste(head(A_ov %>% group_by(to) %>% summarise(n = sum(n)) %>% arrange(desc(n)) %>% pull(to) %>% short_sch(), 3), collapse = ", ")`
— the schools with room, not the schools nearest the refusal.

## This is where displacement comes from

The strategic view's **displacement** measure is the difference between
the two quantities this section connects: what a neighbourhood's children
wanted, and what they were offered. A child who is counted as displaced
is a child who appears somewhere in the chart above.

```{r ov-displaced}
#| tbl-cap: "The neighbourhoods losing most children to the ceiling, 2026. Displacement is demand that was refused, wherever it ended up."
d_ai %>%
  mutate(lost = pmax(wanted - flow, 0)) %>%
  group_by(zone) %>%
  summarise(Oi = first(Oi), catchment = first(catchment),
```
